title: Streetlights Are Making Thousands of Pill Bugs March in Creepy Circles
summary: Imagine you're a tiny pill bug, also called a roly-poly. You like dark, damp places under rocks. But one night, a streetlight flicks on, and suddenly you can't help but join a huge, spinning circle with thousands of other bugs. That's exactly what scientists discovered in Israel! A nature lover first noticed these creepy "death spirals" on summer nights. Researchers found that the bugs, a species called Armadillo sordidus, are drawn to the edge of the light circle on the ground. Once they reach the bright border, they start walking along it. As more bugs arrive, the line becomes a rotating ring. One circle had over 5,000 pill bugs! Why is this bad? Most of the marchers were females carrying eggs. They weren't looking for mates; they were just trapped. The nonstop walking wastes energy and pulls them away from their safe, moist hiding spots. In one case, a centipede sneaked in and ate some of the distracted bugs. Scientists tested different lights and magnets, but only white light shining straight down caused the swirl. The circular shape of the light beam is the key—it creates a boundary that the bugs' instincts tell them to follow. This shows how a simple human invention, the streetlight, can mess up the ancient behaviors of small creatures. Next time you see a streetlight, think about the tiny dramas unfolding in its glow!
why_it_matters: This reminds you that even things we think are harmless, like a streetlight, can puzzle the creatures around us, so being aware of nature at night matters for protecting tiny neighbors.

keywords.explanation: A species is a specific kind of living thing, like a pill bug type with the scientific name Armadillo sordidus.
Death spirals are creepy circles of thousands of pill bugs walking around and around under a streetlight until they are exhausted.
A boundary is an edge or border, like the line between the bright light and the dark ground.
Instincts are built-in behaviors animals are born with; the bugs instinctively followed the light’s edge.
A centipede is a long, many-legged predator that hunted the distracted pill bugs in the spiral.
Circular means round, like the shape of the light beam on the ground that trapped the bugs.

background_read: Many animals are attracted to artificial light at night — moths circle porch lights, sea turtles crawl toward bright hotels instead of the ocean, and now pill bugs show a new, strange effect.
Pill bugs are not insects; they are isopods, a type of crustacean related to shrimp and crabs that have adapted to life on land. They breathe with gills, so they need damp places to survive.

The circular shape of a streetlight’s beam on the ground creates a sharp border. The bugs’ instinct to follow edges makes them walk along it endlessly, which shows how even simple human inventions can upset natural behaviors.
Article_Structure: WHO: A nature lover first noticed it, then scientists studied the pill bugs (Armadillo sordidus) in Israel.
WHAT: Under white streetlights, thousands of pill bugs form rotating 'death spirals' — mostly egg-carrying females walking in circles until exhausted.
WHERE: On the ground at night beneath streetlights in Israel.
WHY: The circular light boundary triggers the bugs’ edge-following instinct, showing how artificial light can accidentally harm small creatures.

perspectives.description: People who care about animals can use this discovery to design streetlights that don’t trap bugs — for example, using shields or different colors of light.
To most people, a spinning bug circle looks funny or creepy, but scientists see a serious problem showing how deeply humans change the environment without meaning to.
Researchers are curious why only white light from above causes the swirl, and not other lights or magnets. Solving this puzzle might teach us more about how animals sense their world.
